3.0.s.en: Recognizing the One who rose from the dead:

3.0.0.en: After the bride sang, praising the effectiveness of the Cross in her life and declaring that the banquet of the resurrection is the wedding banquet, during which she enjoys union with the Bridegroom and her inner depths set out toward His final coming, she reviewed, in a symbolic picture, the events of the resurrection as they concern her, and said:

3.0.1.en: "By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not; I called him, but he gave me no answer. I will rise now, and go about the city in the streets, and in the broad ways I will seek him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not. The watchmen that go about the city found me: to whom I said, Saw ye him whom my soul loveth?

3.0.2.en: It was but a little that I passed from them, but I found him whom my soul loveth: I held him, and would not let him go, until I had brought him into my mother's house, and into the chamber of her that conceived me.

3.0.3.en: I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds (mighty ones) of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please" [1-5].

3.0.4.en: We can interpret this speech from two points of view: as the speech of the Catholic Church to her Bridegroom Christ, or as the speech of the soul, as a member of the Church, with her Christ.

3.1.s.en: 1. The first interpretation: the speech of the Catholic Church:

3.1.0.en: This symbolic speech carries a living picture of the events of the resurrection as they concern the Church since her Bridegroom was lifted up on the Cross; she sought Him three times and did not find Him except the last time.

3.1.1.en: a. The first time she sought Him "by night," and perhaps this is a reference to the darkness that covered the earth at the moments of the Cross, for the Scripture says: "Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land unto the ninth hour. And about the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice... and, behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom; and the earth did quake, and the rocks rent; and the graves were opened; and many bodies of the saints which slept arose" (Mt 27:45-52).

3.1.2.en: The day became night, and there was darkness over all the land, and not even the disciples were able to grasp the mystery of salvation at that time... for they had not yet enjoyed the enlightenment. They sought Him on their beds and did not find Him, and they called Him and He did not answer them. They sought Him in the darkness of fleshly human thinking, on their beds, unable to strive with Him or to grasp the mysteries of the Spirit, so they did not find Him. Perhaps they were asking within their thoughts: Is this the Messiah, the Savior?! Or, in the words of the two disciples of Emmaus afterward: "We trusted that it had been he which should have redeemed Israel" (Lk 24:21). Perhaps they expected that He would escape from the hands of those who crucified Him and avenge Himself and establish His kingdom at that time, but nothing of this happened at all!

3.1.3.en: b. The second time the bride sought Him by night, not on her bed but, as she said: "I will rise now, and go about the city in the streets, and in the broad ways," and this is a reference to the state of the disciples after the Lord was buried and they entered the upper room and all their time turned into night, for they sought the Lord while afraid, with the doors shut. They tried to regain their strength, and they rose and searched for Him in the city, in the streets and the broad ways. It was the Sabbath, but they did not taste the flavor of rest, nor were they able to be still; rather their upper room, not the city, was turned, and their thoughts and perhaps their conversations together were turned into streets and broad ways, each one asking within himself or with his companions: And what is the end of the matter?! They searched for Him among themselves and were tossed about in their depths, and there was no peace!

3.1.4.en: c. In the third time the search for Him was accomplished at the empty tomb, for Mary went out at dawn on Sunday while the darkness remained; she did not care to walk in the streets and broad ways until she passed by the tomb. She went out on behalf of the Church with a sorrowful heart and asked the angel with tears about Him whom her soul loved, and she had scarcely passed him when she saw the Lord and clung to Him... She held Him at first, but when she wished to remain so, He asked her to hasten and tell the disciples to meet Him in Galilee... as though St. Mary had brought Him into the Church, the house of her mother and the chamber of her that conceived her.

3.1.5.en: As for the speech of the Church: "I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds (mighty ones) of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please," it is a speech of reproach filled with love, directed from the Christian Church to the company of the Jews. They mocked the Bridegroom on the Cross, saying: "If thou be the Son of God, come down from the cross" (Mt 27:40), and the chief priests also, mocking with the scribes and elders, said: "He saved others; himself he cannot save. If he be the King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him" (Mt 27:41-42). It is as though the Church, after entering into His resurrection, returned to say to the daughters of Jerusalem: Why were you hastening the Bridegroom to arise? I charge you by the prophets, "the roes and the hinds of the field," to leave Him to arise on the third day wherever He pleases! If He has slept on the Cross, then review the prophecies and remember that He rises when He pleases! I have now come to know the mystery of His death and burial: He died by power, and rose to raise us with Him!

3.2.s.en: 2. The second interpretation: the speech of the human soul:

3.2.0.en: If the Church sought Him three times, while He was on the Cross, while He was in the tomb, and finally after His resurrection at the empty tomb... and on the third day she found Him, then the human soul in her search for Him may seek Him three times or in three ways, but she does not find Him except in the last way: she seeks Him by her own effort, or she seeks Him through the servants alone, and finally she seeks Him with confidence in the possibilities of God's work in her, without ignoring her own striving or the service of the workers in His vineyard.

3.2.1.en: a. Seeking the Lord by one's own human effort: The soul began her speech: "By night on my bed..." Perhaps in her time of weakness she dreamed a troubling dream that she had lost her Bridegroom, so she went out to search for Him by her own effort, but she cannot meet with Him unless He draws her to Himself.

3.2.2.en: Perhaps by night she meant that she had become slack in the darkness of recklessness, seeking Him while lying on her bed in idle dependence without true spiritual striving... Therefore she sought Him and did not find Him. She did not rest on the bed which she described before: "our bed is green" (Song 1:16), but she wanted to lie on her own human bed.

3.2.3.en: We saw that the speech about "our green bed" refers to the union of God the Word with our humanity, as He took our body into Himself, whereas the speech about "my bed" or "my couch" refers to "my body" or "my humanity" in its isolation or its self-reliance. St. Augustine sought the Lord while lying on his couch when he went out to search for Him in pride and did not find Him, for he said: [I shut the door of my God against myself... and when I wished to knock that it might be opened to me, I was working all the more to make it fast shut, because I dared to search in pride for Him whom only the humble know... While I was perishing I thought I was able to fly, so I left the nest and fell before I could fly, but the God of mercy raised me up so that passers-by would not trample me with their feet to death, and He put me in the nest].

3.2.4.en: St. Gregory, Bishop of Nyssa, sees that she calls Him here "him whom my soul loveth" and does not give Him a name, because when she sought Him by a name, Him who cannot be named, she did not find Him... She asked about Him the angelic powers who were gathered together praising in countless numbers, and they fell silent... for she seeks Him who cannot be comprehended in a limited, comprehending way... and in their silence she realized her error. Therefore she is careful now not to give Him any title.

3.2.5.en: b. In the second stage the soul went out from herself, for she left her bed saying "I will rise," and entered the city to search for her Bridegroom, searching for Him within the city in the streets and the broad ways.

3.2.6.en: Augustine went out to the streets and broad ways by searching for God through the books of the philosophers, and in the streets by searching for Him in nature, but he did not find God, for in his foolishness he went out to seek God outside himself, although God was within him, deeper than his depths and higher than his height.

3.2.7.en: Perhaps the city here refers to the Holy Bible, so the soul entered the streets and broad ways of the Scripture, that is, its symbols and prophecies, and yet she was not able to meet her Bridegroom, because she did not ask for the help of God who draws her to Himself. This is what the chief priests and scribes of the people did when they searched in the Scripture and learned about the Messiah that He would be born in Bethlehem of Judea (Mt 2:4-6), informing Herod of this without themselves meeting their Christ!

3.2.8.en: c. In the third stage she searched for Him through "the watchmen," who are the servants of the divine Word, and this time also she is not able to meet her Bridegroom except after passing them a little. For the workers in the vineyard support the soul to enter to the Bridegroom, but they cannot bring her in to Him except by His own work, for He alone is able to draw the heart toward Himself.

3.2.9.en: Truly, the priests are committed to keeping watch, but "Except the LORD keep the city, the watchmen wake but in vain" (Ps 27:1). If they perform the priestly work, it is through the Bridegroom Himself, "a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek."

3.2.10.en: The Apostle Paul realized his people's obligation to pass beyond him and his companions, for he affirmed to the Corinthians: "Who then is Paul, and who is Apollos?... I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase" (1 Cor 3:5-6).

3.2.11.en: In Christ Jesus Himself the soul experiences union with Him, so she enters by Him into her depths, into the inner heart; they commune together far from all eyes, revealing their secrets to one another without affectation!

3.2.12.en: She asks the daughters of Jerusalem, that is, those who are close to her, to leave her with her Bridegroom in a life of stillness and hidden prayer... for she wishes that nothing distract her from remaining in the arms of this life-giving Bridegroom.

3.3.0.en: The troubling dream has ended and the darkness has dispersed by the resurrection of the Lord, so we recognized Him and enjoyed union with Him, and the mark of His "resurrection" became ours. Therefore the angels stood as friends of the Bridegroom who rose from the dead, singing and praising the bride who has risen with her Bridegroom, saying:

3.3.1.en: "Who is this that cometh out of the wilderness like pillars of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, with all powders of the merchant?" [6].

3.3.2.en: It is noticed that this speech cannot apply to carnal love, otherwise what would be the connection between it and the speech preceding it? For at the beginning of the chapter we see the bride slack on her bed seeking her Bridegroom and not finding Him, and after the effort she met Him and brought Him into her mother's house, and now we suddenly see her described as coming up from the wilderness perfumed with myrrh and frankincense and adorned with all the cosmetics (powders) bought from the merchant... Would she bring Him into her mother's house and leave Him to go out with perfumes and adornment?! But it is a wonderful spiritual speech, for the bride, having met her Bridegroom who rose from the dead and ascended to His heavens, brought Him into her heart... and the natural fruit of this work was that she ascended with Him and by Him to His heavens, as the Apostle Paul says: "hath raised us up together, and made us sit together in heavenly places." His entering into her depths lifted her above the wilderness of this life, so she communed with Him: "I have a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better" (Phil 1:23).

3.3.3.en: Perhaps these words "Who is this that cometh up...?" come from the Bridegroom Himself, who supports her and encourages her, assuring her that He sees her ascending to the heavens although she is now on earth. While still in the body she has become like the smoke that carries the fragrance of sweet prayer, in which are the breaths of the Bridegroom Himself. And perhaps they are the words of the heavenly ones who looked upon the earthly human beings, when the door of Paradise was opened before them and they set out with the Lord Christ dwelling in them, rising from day to day toward the heavenly things; and perhaps also the words of the daughters of Jerusalem, those who were formerly reproaching the Church for her blackness, as we saw before, because of her not belonging to the fathers and the prophets... since she is of the Gentiles, but she now appears, through her union with the Messiah the Savior, beautiful and radiant, ascending from glory to glory.!

3.4.0.en: In the old days the people of Israel wandered forty years in the wilderness, in which they were exposed to the bites of deadly serpents because of their disobedience and murmuring, and the Gentiles were bound to the wilderness of the world and were defiled with evils... But now the believers have been united with the Messiah, who alone is able to bring man out of the wilderness of this world to the freedom of the heavenly Kingdom, as the Lord Himself says: "And no man hath ascended up to heaven, but he that came down from heaven, even the Son of man which is in heaven" (Jn 3:13). And as St. John Chrysostom says: [We who were formerly unworthy of earthly glory now ascend to the Kingdom of Heaven, and enter the heavens, and take our place before the divine throne].

3.5.0.en: In the old days God used to descend upon Mount Sinai and it smoked, a sign of the splendor of His glory and His power (Ex 19:18; 20:18; Ps 104:32; 144:5), and when His glory descended in His holy house, whether the Tabernacle or the Temple, the place was filled with smoke (Isa 6:4; cf. Rev 15:8). But now that the heart of the believer has opened to the Lord, his very life has become a glory to God, it has become a sweet smoke ascending from the wilderness of this world and rising toward heaven.

3.5.1.en: The smoke used to signify God's coming down and His presence to give a promise to His beloved ones, as He did with Abram when he divided the bloody sacrifices in the midst and the Lord entered with him into living promises, for a smoking furnace and a burning lamp passed between the pieces (Gen 15:17); but now the Lord has dwelt in the heart of His people and set out with them like smoke, not that they may hear promises from God but that they may enjoy God Himself, their portion and their inheritance.

3.5.2.en: The smoke also used to signify the Lord's presence to sanctify His people, as the prophet Isaiah says: "When the Lord shall have washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion, and shall have purged the blood of Jerusalem from the midst thereof by the spirit of judgment, and by the spirit of burning. And the LORD will create upon every dwelling place of mount Zion, and upon her assemblies, a cloud and smoke by day, and the shining of a flaming fire by night" (Isa 4:4-5); but now that the Church has been sanctified in the blood of Christ and washed in the waters of Baptism, the fire of the Holy Spirit has kindled her, so she has become a holy smoke rising to where Christ sits.

3.5.3.en: The smoke signifies the life of prayer, as St. John the Theologian says: "And the smoke of the incense, which came with the prayers of the saints, ascended up before God out of the angel's hand" (Rev 8:4)... Therefore it is said in the Song of Songs that she who ascends is like pillars of incense, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense... because frankincense is a symbol of the life of prayer.

3.5.4.en: At any rate, it is not a smoke that fills the world with suffocation, a sign of God's anger (Deut 29:20; Isa 34:10; Rev 9:2; 14:11; 18:9, 18; 19:3), so that she would be like Sodom and Gomorrah where the smoke of the land went up as the smoke of a furnace (Gen 19:28). Nor does it carry the sign of weakness and death, as the prophet says: "the heavens shall vanish away like smoke" (Isa 51:6), and the psalmist's saying: "For my days are consumed in smoke" (Ps 102), nor the sign of the evil and sloth which spoil the inner sight, as the wise man says: "As smoke to the eyes, so is the sluggard to them that send him" (Prov 10:26).

3.5.5.en: That smoke chokes the soul and spoils the eyes, but the bride is pillars of perfumed smoke that gladden heaven and delight it, and the materials of her perfume are: 1. Myrrh, because she was buried with Christ Jesus, who was wrapped with myrrh and spices; for if she is not buried with Him she cannot enjoy the new life, risen and lifted toward the heavens, as the Apostle says: "Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life" (Rom 6:4). We are buried in Baptism, and our old man dies, and we are born a new, spiritual birth, so that by the Holy Spirit we may be lifted up to our heavenly Father.

3.5.6.en: On this St. John Chrysostom says: [It is not by a mother and a father, not by the lying down of men, nor by the pains of labor that we are born again, but from the Holy Spirit our new tissues are made, and in the water they are formed, and from the water we are born mystically as from the womb... The womb needs much time for the body to be formed in it, but from the water and the Spirit the life of the Spirit is formed in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye! That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit (Jn 3:6)].

3.5.7.en: He says also: [When the head is plunged under the water as in a tomb, our whole old humanity is poured out into it... and when you come out after that, it floats and comes out, our man made new. And as it is easy for us to plunge and then to float, so it is easy for God to bury the old humanity and clothe us with the new man]. 2. Frankincense, for the fragrance of the incense of her prayers ascends toward the Lord... and she even repeats with the psalmist: "But I give myself unto prayer." In her union with the One who rose from the dead she comes to know the life of true worship or "unceasing prayer." 3. All the powders of the merchant, which are the cosmetics that the soul buys from Christ Himself, "the Merchant," who alone is able to adorn the soul and beautify her as a bride for Himself.

3.5.8.en: Thus the soul needs to be perfumed by Baptism and to lean on the Holy Spirit, to live her life as unceasing prayer, and to cast herself into the arms of her Bridegroom that He may adorn her... By this she is worthy to be presented as a bride adorned for her husband (Rev 21:2).

3.6.s.en: The time of the wedding banquet:

3.6.0.en: "Behold his bed, which is Solomon's; threescore valiant men are about it, of the valiant of Israel. They all hold swords, being expert in war:

3.6.1.en: every man hath his sword upon his thigh because of fear in the night.

3.6.2.en: King Solomon made himself a throne of the wood of Lebanon.

3.6.3.en: He made the pillars thereof of silver, the bottom thereof of gold, the seat of it of purple, the midst thereof being paved with love, for the daughters of Jerusalem" [7-10].

3.6.4.en: If the Cross of the Lord and His resurrection are the mystery of the wedding banquet, as the Bridegroom who rose from the dead comes forward and raises His bride who entered with Him into the circle of His sufferings and crucifixion, and dwells in her heart so that she ascends by Him to heaven, perfumed and adorned with all spiritual beauty, we ask: When will this be? Or what is the time of the banquet.?

3.6.5.en: The answer came carrying two aspects: a temporal aspect and an eternal one. We enter into the procession of the Bridegroom and His banquet in the time of our sojourn, in the night of this world, to fight the terrors of the night, striving even to blood, and we enjoy His eternal procession in the day that has no night, where we sit at His right hand, partakers with Him in glory. Therefore the Bridegroom appears in two processions, one in the night where He sets up the bed in the midst of His striving children, and the other in the day, seated on His eternal throne. 1. The temporal procession: In this procession the Bridegroom appears with sixty valiant men around Him, all men of war, carrying their swords upon their thighs, striving amid the terrors of the night of this life. It is the procession that the striving Church lives around Christ her Bridegroom.

3.6.6.en: Here the Bridegroom appears having set up a "bed" in the midst of the Church, but it is not like the bed of the bride who lay on it in the night (Song 3:1), seeking her Bridegroom in slackness and not finding Him, calling Him and He does not answer her! Nor like the beds into which the frogs came up (Ex 8:3), a sign of God's anger and His plagues on Pharaoh, nor like the beds on which men lie when they give up the spirit and lie without movement (Gen 49:33; 2 Kgs 1:4), nor like the bed which David the psalmist made to swim with tears every night (Ps 6:6); rather it is a unique bed on which "the Lion that came out of the tribe of Judah" couched (cf. Gen 49:9), it is the Cross of the Lord which brought about peace for the Church, for by it heaven was reconciled with earth, and it gave victory and triumph to the Church over the spiritual powers of evil.

3.6.7.en: "Solomon" set it up to declare that it is the mystery of the Church's peace and the sign of her rest; on it the Apostle Peter rested secretly in the prison and slept without disturbance until the angel came to wake him and bring him out (Acts 12:6-10)... He gives His beloved sleep... that is, peace.!

3.6.8.en: Our true Solomon set up a bed in the midst of His people so that He may sleep continually within the ship of our life (Mt 8:24; Mk 4:38), so we do not perish, whatever severe disturbances occur in the sea.

3.6.9.en: And to show that it is the bed of spiritual rest and inner peace without slackness or sloth, the Song of Songs shows us that around it are sixty valiant men, all holding swords and expert in war, every man with his sword upon his thigh because of the terrors of the night. Around the Cross the striving Church gathers as men of war, so that as He overcame, they also overcome by Him and with Him. Every believer carries upon his thigh his sword, which is the word of God, that he may overcome, as it is written in the Book of Revelation: "And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb (that is, by the Cross), and by the word of their testimony (the word of God); and they loved not their lives unto the death" (Rev 12:11).

3.6.10.en: Who are the sixty valiant men of the valiant of Israel who surround Him? They are the sons of the Kingdom, the new, spiritual Israel, the chosen ones who accepted the Cross and entered with God into a new covenant. These came to the banquet in the pampering of love but without softness; rather they armed themselves with the sword of the Spirit and the helmet of salvation, striving even to blood against sin without relenting. Therefore the Apostle Paul advises us, saying: "Finally, my brethren, be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might. Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil. For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places. Wherefore take unto you the whole armour of God... Stand therefore, having your loins girt about with truth, and having on the breastplate of righteousness; and your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace; above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked. And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God" (Eph 6:10-17).

3.6.11.en: As for the mystery of their number, 60, we know that the number 12 signifies the Kingdom of God on earth, for St. Augustine says that the Holy Trinity (3) reigns over the four corners of the world (4). Thus the Kingdom of God on earth means 3 x 4 (12). Therefore the tribes of the children of Israel were twelve, and the number of the disciples of the New Testament is twelve, and the number of the gates of Jerusalem is twelve gates. St. Gregory, Bishop of Nyssa, sees that each one of them carried five swords, which are the sanctification of the five senses by Christ Jesus our Lord, so the number is (12 x 5 = 60). It is as though all those who have become members of His Kingdom have had their senses sanctified in perfection in Christ Jesus.

3.6.12.en: St. Gregory, Bishop of Nyssa, says that the sword of the eye is to look continually toward the Lord, that it may see uprightly and not be defiled by anything; and the sword of hearing is to listen to spiritual things and not to give ear to vanity... and likewise for taste, touch and smell, all this is sanctified by the sword of self-control and contact with the Lord Christ and the breathing of His sweet fragrance... By this man fights all the darkness of sin. 2. The eternal procession: In the temporal procession the Bridegroom appeared on His bed to give His people assurance that He is the mystery of their rest and peace amid their striving in this world or in this temporal life, but in the eternal procession there is no war and no striving, so He appears as a king carried on a throne or a litter borne on arms... He appears on His eternal throne which is borne by the four living creatures (Rev 4).

3.6.13.en: And what is this throne but the Church herself, within whom the Lord dwells and upon whom He sits enthroned forever, and her marks are:

3.6.14.en: a. She is united with the Cross of the Lord and has become one with Him, therefore she is described as made of wood. Her suffering and crucifixion with the Lord remains the mystery of her life and her eternal glory, for the Apostle says: "if so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together" (Rom 8:17).

3.6.15.en: b. As for her being of the wood of Lebanon, we have seen that Lebanon is famous for its cedar, known for its uprightness and sweet fragrance; so the Church of Christ, which lived in her sojourn with uprightness, not halting between two ways, God and the world, carries the fragrance of Christ her Bridegroom.

3.6.16.en: c. Her pillars are of silver, the work of our Solomon Himself. And silver signifies in the Holy Bible the word of God refined seven times, as though the shepherds of the Church and her servants have become pillars in her by their hiding themselves and mingling with the word of God...

3.6.17.en: d. The golden base signifies that the people, having carried the Lord Christ in their practical life, have become heavenly (gold), living on earth as though they were angels of God. Or, as the Apostle says: "that both they that have wives be as though they had none; and they that weep, as though they wept not; and they that rejoice, as though they rejoiced not; and they that buy, as though they possessed not; and they that use this world, as though they used it not" (1 Cor 7:29-31).

3.6.18.en: e. The purple seat signifies the nature of the Church as a queen united with the eternal King.

3.6.19.en: f. Her midst is paved with love for the daughters of Jerusalem, since the Church bears the mark of her Bridegroom, who is love, for the salvation of mankind.

3.7.0.en: "Go forth, O ye daughters of Zion, and behold king Solomon with the crown wherewith his mother crowned him in the day of his espousals, and in the day of the gladness of his heart" [11].

3.7.1.en: This is the invitation which the Church directs to the world to enjoy the banquet of the Cross. She asks mankind to go out from itself, from the ego... "Go forth," so that they may be able to enjoy the sight of the true King, "the new Solomon," whom the nation of the Jews crowned with a crown of thorns.

3.7.2.en: Through spiritual insight the believers see the secret crown of the Crucified One, namely "the forgiveness of our sins and the removal of the curse."

3.7.3.en: This is the day of His wedding and the day of the gladness of His heart, for He offered His blood as a dowry for His bride!
